source.title: "Alexa, can you forget me?" Machine Unlearning Benchmark in Spoken Language Understanding
source.authors: Alkis Koudounas; Claudio Savelli; F. Giobergia; Elena Baralis

record.tranche_reason: The study benchmarks speaker-data unlearning in spoken-language-understanding models, but does not test whether knowledge is recovered by fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, or prompting. Its membership-inference measurements are not those recovery behaviors.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many benchmark results for speaker-level unlearning, including forget-set F1, test-set F1, and membership-inference attack (MIA) scores. These concern a related privacy-unlearning setting, not the targeted-knowledge recovery behaviors in versions A–F. The authors' explicit result about memorization after different training durations is recorded below. The other benchmark scores are not rows for the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study benchmarks eight speaker-data unlearning methods on speech intent-classification models (wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, XLS-R) using forget/test F1 and membership-inference scores. It applies no recovery attack (relearning, activation ablation, quantization, prompting), and the systems are not LLMs with targeted hazardous or factual knowledge. Its results therefore do not bear on versions A–F. The closest finding, that MIA stays near the original after long training, is a related construct about incomplete unlearning, not recovery.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors introduce UnSLU-BENCH and the GUM metric. They find that NG is the most well-rounded method, mainly through efficiency, and that methods differ in efficacy and cost. In the SLURP* experiment, longer training (60 epochs) leaves persistent memorization, with MIA close to the original model.
record.recipe_differences: The paper benchmarks speaker-data unlearning methods in spoken-language-understanding models; it does not use the claim's recovery-attack recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: In the SLURP* training-duration experiment, MIA outcomes vary with the number of training epochs.

fits_no_version.finding: For wav2vec 2.0 on SLURP* with NG+ (LR 5e-07), longer original training (60 epochs) leaves forget-set MIA near the original model (.611 vs .628; gold .506). Shorter training (5–15 epochs) yields MIA near gold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In speech intent classifiers, speaker-level unlearning leaves more membership signal when the original model was trained longer (overfit).

fits_no_version.finding: Across datasets, CF-k leaves MIA well above gold (e.g. .612–.624 vs .493–.520 on SpeechMASSIVE), which the authors call incomplete unlearning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Last-layer-only unlearning leaves speaker membership signal largely intact in SLU models.

record.problems: The study's target is speaker-data membership in SLU models, not recoverability of targeted knowledge in LLMs. MIA does not measure the listed recovery attacks. The paper does not report uncertainty estimates for the recorded results.
record.rows_left_out: The separate method-by-model results in Tables 1–3, including F1 and MIA scores, are not cataloged as rows because they measure speaker-level unlearning outcomes rather than any listed knowledge-recovery behavior. No rows were omitted due to the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No LLM, no targeted-knowledge accuracy near chance, and no recovery attacks.
No relearning or fine-tuning recovery attack.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of blocking versus deletion.
No prompting, rephrasing, jailbreak or cross-lingual recovery test.
No method is tested for resistance to recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: Rows correctly excluded from all versions. Benchmark Tables 1–3 are appropriately left out, since they measure speaker-membership MIA, not knowledge recovery. The study cites Who's Harry Potter? only as background.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether targeted knowledge is brought near chance while retaining general ability and whether the specified recovery attacks fail.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of access-blocking versus deletion.
No prompt-rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery test.
No newer method is tested for resistance to the specified recovery attacks.
